notes.b: Development varies between continents, countries, regions within a country and districts within cities.
points: The Brandt Line, from the Brandt Report North–South: A Programme for Survival (1980), separates the rich North from the poorer South.
The Brandt Commission was chaired by the former West German Chancellor Willy Brandt. The line runs roughly along 30°N, dipping south to put Australia and New Zealand in the North.
The North (North America, Europe, Russia, Japan, Australia and New Zealand) is richer than the South (Latin America, Africa and most of Asia).
The line is a simplification: Singapore, South Korea and the Gulf states are rich although they lie in the South.
The terms First World and Third World are outdated; the critique of them belongs to the Global Interdependence option.

Global inequality is extreme: the richest tenth of the world's people own about 76% of global wealth, and the poorest half own about 2% (World Inequality Report 2022). The justice angle is in the Global issues and a justice perspective note.

notes.h: The pattern of HDI across the world
points: Very high HDI is found in Europe, North America, Australia, Japan and the Gulf.
High and medium HDI cover most of Latin America, East and South-East Asia and North Africa.
Low HDI is concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, with Afghanistan, Yemen and Haiti outside Africa. Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas.
The named rankings and categories are in the Measuring economic development note.
Luxembourg has the highest GDP per head in the EU, and Bulgaria the lowest (Eurostat, early 2020s).
Luxembourg's GDP per head is inflated by cross-border commuters, so it overstates living standards there.
The EU's core is a richer north-west belt, the Blue Banana, and its periphery lies in the east and south. The core and periphery terms are explained in the Socio-economic regions note.

Within member states, Italy's Mezzogiorno is about 22% of Italy's GDP, with GDP per head a little over half that of the Centre-North in recent years (see A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno).
Romania and Bulgaria contain many of the EU's less developed regions.
An EU less developed region has GDP per head under 75% of the EU average, and such regions receive most of the EU's cohesion funding.
The Dublin region has the highest disposable income per person in the State. The Border and Midland regions are consistently among the lowest (CSO county income figures, 2010s to 2020s).
County Dublin has about 1.45 million of the State's about 5.1 million people (Census 2022).
Dublin's advantages are its capital and port functions, multinational and financial-services investment, universities and the airport, which together provide most of the high-value jobs.
The West and North-West are peripheral, with remoteness, weaker infrastructure, dependence on farming and small firms, and out-migration (see A Peripheral Irish Region).
Peripheral location does not by itself mean poverty: the West is peripheral within a very rich country.

notes.h: Irish regional policy and transport investment
points: The BMW region held Objective 1 status for 2000 to 2006.
Three regional assemblies have operated since 2015: Northern and Western; Southern; and Eastern and Midland.
Project Ireland 2040, launched in February 2018, combines the National Planning Framework and the National Development Plan.

The National Planning Framework aims for the Northern and Western and Southern regions together to grow as much as the Eastern and Midland region, and for half of future population growth to go to the five cities: Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford.
Metrolink is a planned metro line from Swords, via Dublin Airport, to Dublin city centre.
The National Broadband Plan (contract signed 2019) aims to bring high-speed broadband to rural homes.

Transport investment can reduce regional income differences: better access attracts firms to regional towns, cuts costs and commuting times, and widens the job market. It also reduces congestion, shortens journeys and lowers emissions.
Even rich places contain pockets of deprivation, and poor regions exist within richer countries.
India: Census 2011 literacy was about 94% in Kerala and about 62% in Bihar. Fertility was about 1.8 in Kerala and about 3.0 in Bihar (NFHS-5, 2019 to 2021); see the India note.
Brazil: the poor North-East contrasts with the rich South-East; see the Case study of a developing economy note.

notes.h: Physical factors: climate, disease, relief and soils
notes.b: Physical factors affect development by limiting or supporting farming, health and transport. They influence development but do not determine it.
points: The Sahel, the semi-arid belt south of the Sahara (Mali, Niger, Chad and Burkina Faso), has suffered repeated droughts since the 1970s, which limit farming and cause famine.
In Ethiopia, outside the Sahel, drought worsened by civil war led to the 1984 to 1985 famine, followed by Live Aid in 1985.
Extreme heat and tropical storms add difficulty; temperate climates suit productive farming.
Climate does not decide development: Singapore is tropical, yet it is one of the world's richest countries. Botswana shows that a poor start can be overcome.
Malaria and other tropical diseases reduce life expectancy, the productivity of workers and children's schooling; the malaria figure is in the Measuring economic development note.
Mountains, deserts and poor soils limit farming and make transport costly, while fertile lowlands and river plains support dense populations and farming surpluses.

notes.h: Physical factors: location, resources and hazards
points: Landlocked countries depend on neighbours' roads and ports, which raises trade costs. Landlocked developing countries include Chad, Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Malawi, Uganda, Afghanistan and Bolivia.
Coastal countries with good harbours trade more easily. Peripheral location adds to transport costs for Ireland and for the EU's outlying regions.
Natural resources can fund development: Botswana's diamonds were discovered at Orapa in 1967 and are mined by Debswana, a joint venture of the government and De Beers.
Norway's oil has been extracted from the North Sea since the early 1970s, and its sovereign wealth fund, the Government Pension Fund Global, is one of the world's largest.

Resources can also bring the resource curse of corruption, conflict and dependence on one export. Nigeria's oil from the Niger Delta dominates its exports, and oil spills and conflict have affected the Delta.
The DR Congo produces about 70% of the world's cobalt (early 2020s), yet it is one of the poorest countries.
Haiti's earthquake of 12 January 2010, magnitude 7.0, struck near Port-au-Prince and killed over 100,000 people (estimates vary); see the note on the geography of earthquakes.
Floods, cyclones and droughts destroy infrastructure and set poor countries back for years, while rich countries recover faster.

notes.h: Social factors: population, education, health and gender
points: Rapid population growth spreads spending on schools and health thinly and creates more young dependants. Niger has the world's highest fertility rate, about 6 to 7 children per woman (early 2020s).
A falling birth rate can give a demographic dividend, a larger share of working-age people to drive growth.
An educated workforce raises productivity and attracts investment; low literacy, especially among women, holds development back, as the Kerala and Bihar contrast shows.
Disease, malnutrition and HIV/AIDS reduce the workforce and life expectancy, and health spending raises productivity.
Where girls are educated and women work outside the home, families are smaller, children are healthier and household incomes are higher.
Brain drain: doctors, nurses and graduates leave poor countries. Remittances sent home by migrants help offset this; India is the world's largest recipient of remittances (2020s).
Water, sanitation, electricity, roads and internet are both a cause and a result of development.
Attitudes to women's roles and girls' education matter: early marriage reduces schooling and raises fertility.
Social structures and inequality limit opportunity for some groups: caste in India, land concentration in Latin America and ethnic divisions.
Many languages within borders drawn in the colonial period can make national unity and education harder; a world language such as English can help, as in India's IT sector.
The colonial cultural legacy includes European languages, education aimed at a small elite and a culture of exporting raw materials (see the Case study of a developing economy note).
Attitudes to enterprise, saving and education differ between societies: South Korea places a high value on education. Traditional farming practices and land tenure can slow change.

notes.h: Political factors: stability, governance and corruption
points: Political stability and good governance attract investment and allow long-term planning. Botswana became independent in 1966 and has held regular elections as a multi-party democracy since independence.

War destroys infrastructure, displaces people and scares off investors. Syria's civil war from 2011 displaced millions. South Sudan became independent in July 2011 and entered civil war in December 2013; Sudan is covered in the Case study of a developing economy note.
Corruption diverts public money and aid. Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index ranks Denmark at or near the top and Somalia and South Sudan at or near the bottom (2020s).
Colonial history left borders, export economies and weak institutions; the detail is in the Case study of a developing economy note.

Government economic policy matters: education, infrastructure, openness to trade and investment, and industrial policy, as in South Korea, China and Ireland, contrast with mismanagement, as in Zimbabwe and Venezuela.
Debt repayments take money from schools and hospitals, and rich countries' farm subsidies and tariffs disadvantage poor exporters; the detail is in the Global issues and a justice perspective note.
EU membership and funds helped Ireland, Spain and Portugal, all major recipients of EU regional and cohesion funds, to converge with richer states (see the Ireland and the European Union chapter).

notes.h: Change over time: general pattern and theory
points: Development is not fixed: countries can rise, as Ireland, South Korea, China and Botswana have, or fall, as Zimbabwe, Venezuela and Syria have.
A falling HDI is usually caused by war, economic collapse or disease.
Cumulative causation: core regions keep growing because they attract capital and skilled migrants.

Spread effects: growth can sometimes spread from the core to the periphery. Full core–periphery theory is in The Global Economy: Multinationals and Globalisation chapter; models of development are in the Global Interdependence option.
The Korean War (1950 to 1953) left the South among the world's poorest countries.
From the 1960s, under Park Chung-hee, the government planned export-led industrialisation: textiles first, then steel, shipbuilding, cars and electronics.
Chaebol, large family-controlled conglomerates such as Samsung, Hyundai and LG, drove the industrial growth.
The government invested heavily in education. South Korea joined the OECD in 1996.
The 1997 Asian financial crisis hit South Korea hard, but it recovered. UNCTAD reclassified it as a developed country in 2021, and it is now a very high HDI country.
Its growth came from industry and education, not from natural resources.
Economic reforms began in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, known as opening up.
Special Economic Zones were set up from 1980, the first at Shenzhen, beside Hong Kong.
China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001.
The World Bank estimates that close to 800 million Chinese were lifted out of extreme poverty since 1978 (World Bank, 2022).
China has been the world's second-largest economy since 2010, overtaking Japan, but it is upper-middle income, not a developed country.
Coastal provinces are much richer than the western interior, and hundreds of millions of rural people migrated to coastal cities.
Botswana became independent in 1966 as one of the world's poorest countries.
Diamond revenue funded roads, schools and clinics, and stable democratic government and comparatively low corruption helped.
Botswana is now an upper-middle-income country.
HIV/AIDS sharply reduced life expectancy in the 1990s and 2000s; it recovered with free antiretroviral treatment.
Dependence on diamonds is a weakness of the economy.
Heavy emigration in the 1950s: net emigration was about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961.
T. K. Whitaker's Economic Development (1958) led to the First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958), which offered free trade, grants and tax breaks for foreign firms.
Ireland joined the EEC on 1 January 1973.
The Celtic Tiger boom ran from the mid-1990s to 2007. Free secondary education, free trade and foreign investment are described in the Measuring economic development note.
A property crash and banking crisis from 2008 led to an EU–IMF bailout of €85 billion, agreed in November 2010; Ireland exited the programme in December 2013.
Zimbabwe: land seizures from 2000 cut farm output; hyperinflation peaked in 2008, and the Zimbabwe dollar was abandoned in 2009.
Venezuela: the economy depended on oil. After oil prices collapsed in 2014, the economy shrank by well over half, and more than 7 million people emigrated (2024).
Syria: its HDI fell during the civil war that began in 2011, reversing decades of progress.

keyTerms.definition: The line, drawn in the 1980 Brandt Report, that roughly separates the richer North from the poorer South, running along about 30°N.
The richer north-west core of the EU, which contrasts with the poorer periphery in the east and south.
An EU region whose GDP per head is under 75% of the EU average, and which receives most of the EU's cohesion funding.
The semi-arid belt south of the Sahara, where repeated droughts limit farming and cause famine.
The problems, such as corruption, conflict and dependence on one export, that can arise when a country relies on mineral or oil wealth.
The loss of skilled workers, such as doctors, nurses and graduates, who emigrate from poorer countries.
Money sent home by migrants to family in their country of origin.
The economic gain from a falling birth rate, which gives a larger share of working-age people.
The process by which core regions keep growing because they attract capital and skilled migrants.
A large family-controlled conglomerate, such as Samsung or Hyundai, that drove South Korea's industrialisation.
An area with favourable rules for trade and investment, used by China from 1980 to attract foreign firms.
Development strategy that builds manufacturing industries to sell goods to foreign markets.

factCards.term: EU: where GDP per head is highest and lowest, and where the core is

factCards.term: Ireland's regional divide: richest and poorest regions, and why

factCards.term: How transport investment can reduce regional income differences
factCards.definition: Better access attracts firms to regional towns, cuts costs and commuting times and widens the job market; it also eases congestion. factCards.term: Disease, relief and soils: how they affect development
factCards.definition: Malaria and other tropical diseases cut life expectancy, workers' productivity and children's schooling. Mountains, deserts and poor soils limit farming and raise transport costs; fertile lowlands and river plains support dense populations and farm surpluses.

factCards.term: Landlocked countries: why they lag, with named examples
factCards.definition: They depend on neighbours' roads and ports, which raises trade costs, while coastal countries with good harbours trade more easily. Examples: Chad, Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Malawi, Uganda, Afghanistan and Bolivia.

factCards.term: Natural resources: one success and two resource-curse examples
factCards.definition: Norway: North Sea oil since the early 1970s; its sovereign wealth fund is among the world's largest. Nigeria: Niger Delta oil dominates exports, with spills and conflict. DR Congo: about 70% of world cobalt (early 2020s), yet one of the poorest countries.

factCards.term: Haiti 2010: how a natural hazard set development back
factCards.definition: The earthquake of 12 January 2010, magnitude 7.0, struck near Port-au-Prince and killed over 100,000 people (estimates vary). Hazards destroy infrastructure and set poor countries back for years; rich countries recover faster.

factCards.term: Social factors: population growth, education, health and gender
factCards.definition: Fast population growth spreads school and health spending thinly (Niger: about 6 to 7 children per woman); an educated workforce attracts investment, while low female literacy holds development back; disease and HIV/AIDS shrink the workforce; educating girls means smaller, healthier families.

factCards.term: Cultural factors: four that affect development, with examples
factCards.definition: Early marriage cuts girls' schooling and raises fertility; caste in India and land concentration in Latin America limit opportunity; many languages in colonial borders hinder unity, though English helps India's IT sector; South Korea prizes education.

factCards.term: Political stability vs war: three named examples
factCards.definition: Stability: Botswana, independent in 1966, has held regular multi-party elections ever since. War destroys infrastructure and deters investors: Syria's civil war from 2011 made millions refugees; South Sudan, independent July 2011, at war from December 2013.

factCards.term: Corruption and government policy: named examples
factCards.definition: Corruption diverts public money and aid: the Corruption Perceptions Index puts Denmark near the top and Somalia and South Sudan near the bottom (2020s). Good policy helped South Korea, China and Ireland; mismanagement harmed Zimbabwe and Venezuela.

factCards.term: Why a country's HDI falls: three causes, with examples
factCards.definition: War, economic collapse or disease. Syria's HDI fell in the civil war that began in 2011, reversing decades of progress; Zimbabwe and Venezuela suffered economic collapse; HIV/AIDS sharply cut life expectancy in Botswana in the 1990s and 2000s.

factCards.term: South Korea: starting point and how industry was planned
factCards.definition: The Korean War (1950 to 1953) left the South among the world's poorest countries. From the 1960s, under Park Chung-hee, the government planned export-led industrialisation: textiles first, then steel, shipbuilding, cars and electronics.

factCards.term: South Korea: what drove growth, and the milestones since
factCards.definition: Chaebol such as Samsung, Hyundai and LG, and heavy investment in education, not natural resources. Joined the OECD in 1996; hit by the 1997 Asian financial crisis, then recovered; reclassified as a developed country by UNCTAD in 2021; now very high HDI.

factCards.term: China: three reforms that opened its economy
factCards.definition: Economic reforms from 1978 under Deng Xiaoping (opening up); Special Economic Zones from 1980, the first at Shenzhen beside Hong Kong; membership of the World Trade Organization in 2001.

factCards.term: China: results of growth, and the inequality it brought

factCards.term: Botswana: how it rose from poverty after 1966
factCards.definition: Independent in 1966, one of the world's poorest. Diamonds (Orapa, 1967), mined by Debswana (government and De Beers), paid for roads, schools and clinics; stable democracy and comparatively low corruption helped. Now upper-middle income, but diamond-dependent.

factCards.definition: Net emigration was about 400,000 in 1951 to 1961. T. K. Whitaker's Economic Development (1958) led to the First Programme for Economic Expansion: free trade, grants and tax breaks for foreign firms. Free secondary education, 1967; EEC entry, 1 January 1973.

factCards.term: Ireland: Celtic Tiger, crash and bailout dates
factCards.definition: Celtic Tiger boom, mid-1990s to 2007. Property crash and banking crisis from 2008; EU–IMF bailout of €85 billion agreed in November 2010; Ireland exited the programme in December 2013.

factCards.term: Zimbabwe and Venezuela: how their economies collapsed
factCards.definition: Zimbabwe: land seizures from 2000 cut farm output; hyperinflation peaked in 2008; the Zimbabwe dollar was abandoned in 2009. Venezuela: oil-dependent; after the 2014 oil price collapse the economy shrank by well over half and over 7 million emigrated (2024).

questions.prompt: Levels of economic development show major spatial variations. Examine how physical and political factors influence levels of development, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Physical factors shape development by limiting or supporting farming, health and trade. Climate matters: repeated droughts in the Sahel since the 1970s limit farming and cause famine (drought, worsened by civil war, also lay behind the 1984 to 1985 Ethiopian famine), and malaria and other tropical diseases reduce life expectancy and workers' productivity. However, climate does not decide development, since Singapore is tropical and one of the world's richest countries. Location matters: landlocked countries such as Chad, Niger and Mali depend on neighbours' roads and ports, which raises trade costs. Resources can help or harm: Botswana's diamonds funded roads, schools and clinics, while the DR Congo produces about 70% of the world's cobalt yet is one of the poorest countries, and Nigeria's Niger Delta oil dominates exports amid spills and conflict. Hazards can set development back: the Haiti earthquake of 2010 killed over 100,000 people, and rich countries recover faster. Political factors are at least as important. Political stability and good governance attract investment: Botswana has held regular elections since its independence in 1966. War destroys infrastructure and drives away investors: Syria's civil war from 2011 displaced millions, and South Sudan entered civil war in December 2013. Corruption diverts public money and aid, with Somalia and South Sudan at or near the bottom of the Corruption Perceptions Index. Government policy can lift development: South Korea invested in education and planned export-led industry, while mismanagement in Zimbabwe and Venezuela caused collapse. Debt and trade rules also limit poor countries, but these are covered under justice. Overall, physical factors set the conditions, and political choices largely determine whether those conditions are used well.

questions.prompt: Levels of economic development can change over time. Discuss this statement with reference to one country you have studied.
questions.model: South Korea shows that development can rise sharply. The Korean War from 1950 to 1953 left the South among the world's poorest countries. From the 1960s, under Park Chung-hee, the government planned export-led industrialisation, starting with textiles and moving to steel, shipbuilding, cars and electronics. Large family-controlled conglomerates, known as chaebol, such as Samsung, Hyundai and LG, drove the growth. The government invested heavily in education, which gave the workforce the skills that industry needed. South Korea joined the OECD in 1996. Its growth came from industry and education rather than natural resources. The 1997 Asian financial crisis hit the economy hard, but it recovered. UNCTAD reclassified South Korea as a developed country in 2021, and it is now a very high HDI country. The change shows that development is not fixed: the country's starting point was poverty, and deliberate policy changed it within a few decades. The process was not automatic, however. It depended on government planning, a strong education system and the willingness to export to world markets.

questions.prompt: Explain one reason why the Dublin region has the highest disposable income in the State, and one way that investment in transport infrastructure could reduce regional differences in income.
questions.model: The Dublin region has the highest disposable income in the State because it concentrates high-paid jobs: it is the capital, with the main port and airport, and it attracts multinational and financial-services investment and has universities that supply skilled graduates. Investment in transport infrastructure, such as motorways or the planned Metrolink, could reduce regional differences by making regional towns easier to reach. Better access attracts firms to the Border, Midland and Western regions, cuts their costs and commuting times, and widens their job market, so incomes there could rise.
